original_value: Using object-based image analysis (OBIA) techniques for land use-land cover classification (LULC) has become an area of interest due to the availability of high-resolution data and segmentation methods. Multi-resolution segmentation in particular, statistically seen as the most used algorithm, is able to produce non-identical segmentations depending on the required parameters. The total effect of segmentation parameters on the classification accuracy of high-resolution imagery is still an open question, though some studies were implemented to define the optimum segmentation parameters. However, recent studies have not properly considered the parameters and their consequences on LULC accuracy. The main objective of this study is to assess OBIA segmentation and classification accuracy according to the segmentation parameters using different overlap ratios during image object sampling for a predetermined scale. With this aim, we analyzed and compared (a) high-resolution color-infrared aerial images of a newly-developed urban area including different land use types; (b) combinations of multi-resolution segmentation with different shape, color, compactness, bands, and band-weights; and (c) accuracies of classifications based on varied segmentations. The results of various parameters in the study showed an explicit correlation between segmentation accuracies and classification accuracies. The effect of changes in segmentation parameters using different sample selection methods for five main LULC types was studied. Specifically, moderate shape and compactness values provided more consistency than lower and higher values; also, band weighting demonstrated substantial results due to the chosen bands. Differences in the variable importance of the classifications and changes in LULC maps were also explained.

result.paraphrase: This study examines OBIA segmentation and classification accuracy in land use-land cover classification (LULC), motivated by the availability of high-resolution data and segmentation methods. In particular, multi-resolution segmentation—statistically the most widely used algorithm—can yield different segmentations depending on the parameters specified. Although some studies have sought to determine optimal segmentation settings, the overall impact of segmentation parameters on high-resolution image classification accuracy remains unresolved, and recent work has not adequately accounted for these parameters or their effects on LULC accuracy. The study’s main aim is to evaluate OBIA segmentation and classification performance for a predetermined scale by using different overlap ratios during image object sampling. To this end, we analyzed and compared (a) high-resolution color-infrared aerial imagery of a newly developed urban area with multiple land-use types; (b) combinations of multi-resolution segmentation using varying shape, color, compactness, bands, and band weights; and (c) classification accuracies derived from the resulting segmentations. The findings revealed a clear relationship between segmentation accuracy and classification accuracy. For five main LULC classes, the influence of changing segmentation parameters under different sample-selection methods was investigated. Moderate shape and compactness values were more consistent than either lower or higher ones, and band weighting produced strong results depending on the selected bands. The study also describes differences in classification variable importance and the resulting changes in LULC maps.
